The accused-appellants including the condemned prisoners and 8 others namely (1) Sukur Ali, (2) Pradip, (3) Dulal, (Ll) Kalu @ Mashfique, (5) Shimul, (6) Dewan Wadudul Haque, (7) Boby @ Mokaddesur Rahman and (8) Hasan were charged under section 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code for causing the death of Kamal-al- Taslim @ Tara in furtherance 'of their common intention to kill him. 

 "It appears from the facts and attending circumstances and the evidence on record that the moment they saw Tara advancing towards the P.O. to rescue his brother Monu who was already lied down on the ground, common intention to kill Tara developed on the spot in the spur of moment and in furtherance of their common intention to murder accused Kabul, Montu, Sayeedur and Bakkar brutally attacked unarmed Tara, a young promissing student of B.A. class, and in consequence of their brutal attacks the victim died. Accused Kabul and Montu launched their attacks on the occipital region which is the vital part of the human body with intention and knowledge that their dastardly acts would cause death. Injuries caused by accused Sayeedur and Bakkar arc simple in nature, but since they shared the common intention and actively participated in the criminal act they are also liable for an offence of culpable homicide". 

 12. Now coming to the main contention that section 34 of the Penal Code is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case, the learned Advocate has contended that the prosecution has made out no case of common intention within the meaning and scope of section 34 of the Penal Code against the accused-appellants in asmuch as that section requires a pre-arranged plan, and there being no evidence or circumstance to show that any such pre-arranged plan was hatched out, no common intention can be inferred against them and as such the conviction of the accused-appellants under section 302/34 of the Penal Code was not maintainable in law. The learned Advocate referred to the case of Mahbub Shah-Vs-Emperor reported in 49 C.W.N. (P.C.) 678 = AIR 1945 Privy Council 118 and the case of Ekabbar Ali & others -Vs- The State reported in 22 DLR 620 in support of his contention. The learned Advocate further contended that even if the prosecution case is accepted, the accused-appellants may at best be liable for their individual acts committed by them. He has also pointed out that the medical evidence contradicts the ocular testimony in respect of injury No. 2 attributed to condemned prisoner Montu. The learned Deputy Attorney-General Mr. Sultan Ahmad, on the other hand, has contended that the accused-appellants assaulted the victim simultaneously one after another on the vital parts of his body and these circumstances arc sufficient to hold that the accused-appellants developed a common intention to kill the deceased on the spot at the spur of the moment. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submitted that the decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Mahbub Shah -Vs- the Emperor was clarified in a later case by the Judicial Committee in the case of Marnand- Vs-Emperor reported in AIR 1946 Privy Council 45. 

 By an amendment of 1870 the words "in furtherance of common intention of all" have been added to that section which now stands as follows :- 

 "Whenever a criminal act is done by several persons, in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone". 

 14. The crucial test as to the applicability of the principle of vicarious liability under section 34 of the Penal Code is to be found in the phrase "In furtherance of the common intention of all". The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on the interpretation of the scope and meaning of section 34 of the Penal Code held in the case of Mahbub Shah referred to above that common intention implies a prearranged plan and to convict an accused person applying section 34 of the Penal Code it must be proved that a criminal act was done in concert pursuant to the pre-arranged plan and that there should be direct evidence to prove common intention or there must be material to infer from the relevant circumstances that there was such common intention. The Supreme Court of India in the case of Pandurang and others -Vs- State of Hyderabad reported in AIR 1955(S.C.) 216 = 1955 S.C.A. 228 followed the dictum of the Privy Council as laid down in the case of Mahbub Shah and held that common intention pre-supposes prior concert anti it requires a pre-arranged plan before a man can be vicariously convicted for the criminal act of another, the act must be done in furtherance of common intention of them all, so that there be a prior meeting of minds. Both the case of Mahbub Shah and the case of Pandurang were considered by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in the case of Abdur Rahim Mondal -Vs- State reported in 29 DLR (S.C.) 246 wherein their Lordships observed that in these two decisions it. was held that common intention within the meaning of section 34 of the Penal Code pre-supposes prior concert; it also requires pre-arranged plan and care must be taken not to confuse same or similar intention with common intention, the partition which divides "their bounds" is often very thin; nevertheless the distinction is real and substantial and if overlooked will result in miscarriage of justice. Considering the scope of section 34 of the Penal Code their Lordships observed as follows:- 

 "It is well established that a common intention pre-supposes prior concert and it requires a pre-arranged plan because before a man can be vicariously convicted for the criminal act of another the act must have been done in furtherance of common intention of them all. But the prearranged plan need not precede the commission of the crime by a great length of time. A preconcert in the sense of distinguished previous plan is not also necessary to be proved. The, common intention to bring about a particular result may well develop oil the spot as between a number of persons. All that is necessary is either to have direct proof of prior concert or proof of circumstances which necessarily lead to that inference or incriminating acts must be incompatible with the innocence of the accused and incapable of explanation on any other reasonable hypothesis. Further it is the essence of section 34 that the person must be physically present at the actual commission of the crime". 

 15: The Supreme Court of India in the case of Daiya Moshya Bhil- Vs- State of Maharashtra reported in AIR 1984 (S.C) 1717 held that requisite ingredient of common intention within the meaning of section 34 of the Penal Code is that each shared the intention of other and that mere proof of each of the participating culprits having same intention to commit certain act is not sufficient to constitute common intention. 

 16. Thus we find that section 34 lays down the principle of joint liability in the doing of criminal act; the essence of liability is to be found in the existence of common intention animating the accused leading to the doing of a criminal act in furtherance of such intention. For the application of the section it must be shown firstly, that the act was done by several persons, secondly, that all of them intended that the criminal act should be committed and thirdly, that the act was done in furtherance of the common intention shared by all of them. In cases where there is pre-meditation, some kind of pre-concert action, some previous design, and several persons combine and act together they may be deemed to be intending the natural consequence of their combined act; but where the occurrence is sudden, there is commonly a cry for assistance or a call for assault or doing of certain act which is criminal. The person who asked for asistrance or who gave certain order cannot be sure of the pre-action of others. All those who come, may come with different designs and different intentions, Inference of common intention, therefore, should never be reached unless it is a necessary inference from the circumstances of the case. 

 17. Whether or not a criminal act is done by seven persons in furtherance of the common intention of all is a question of fact to be determined on a consideration of the facts in each case and common intention may also be inferred from the circumstances disclosed in the evidence. The simplest method to prove common intention is by direct evidence of that; failing which resort should be had to other circumstances evidencing community of interest. Common intention may be proved by direct evidence such as confessions or an approver's testimony but in most cases its determination depends upon inference from act done, motive possessed by the persons concerned and also [rom the nature of injuries inflicted upon the victim. 

 18. Now let us consider how far the prosecution has been able to prove the common intention of the accused-appellants in causing the death of the deceased by the facts and circumstances proved in the case. The learned Sessions Judge relied upon the evidence of eye witnesses namely, P.Ws. 4, 8, 9, 10 and 11; and considering their evidence along with injuries inflicted upon the deceased held that the accused-appellants shared the common intention and actively participated in the criminal act. So far as the eye witnesses are concerned, they uniformly stated that on the order of accused Bakkar, accused Kabul dealt a 'dao' blow on the head of the deceased followed by a fala blow on the head by accused Montu, which was followed by accused Sayeedur Rahman with an iron rod and accused Bakkar with a sulfi. Mr. Azizul Haque, the learned Advocate for the accused appellants submitted that all the eye witnesses are chance witnesses. But it appears from the evidence that they are independent witnesses and there is no allegation of enmity between them and the accused persons. It is further submitted by the learned Advocate for the accused-appellants that there was no mention in the F.l.R. that accused Bakkar gave any order to catch hold of 'deceased Tara. Mr. Azizul Haque in this connection has referred to the evidence of P.W. 4 wherein he stated that on the order of accused Bakkar accused Kabul, Sayccdur, Montu, Dulal, Sukur, Pradip and Shimul encircled Tara. P.W. 4 has not stated in his evidence the exact words used by accused Bakkar while passing the alleged order. P.W. 8 described the alleged order passed by accused Bakkar using words “এই শালাকেও মারিয়া ফেল” P.W.9 stated in his voidance that accused Bakkar uttered these words: যে বাচাতে আসবে তাকেও খুন করা হবে। P.W. 10 stated that accused Bakkar passed the alieged order by saying, “শালাকে পাওয়া গেছে শেষ করো” and P. W. 11 state that accused Bakkar said এই শালাকেও শেষ করিয়া দাও while pass 109 the alleged order. Thus it appears that five eye witnesses described differently the words used by accused Bakkar in passing the alleged order. Moreover, this fact has not been mentioned in the F.LR Although F.I.R. is not a substantive piece of evidence it has some importance being the earliest recorded version of the prosecution case. It therefore appears to us that the prosecution story of giving order by accused Bakkar is a doubtful one. Moreover, it appears from the evidence of the doctor, P.W. 6 that toninjury Nos. 1 & 2 being the head injuries are responsible for causing the death of the deceased while injury Nos. 3 & 4 attributed to accused Sayeedur Rahman and Bakkar are of simple nature. Inference of common intention of all the accused-appellants cannot be drawn from the different nature of injuries attributed to different accused persons, and the law is that no inference of common intention should be reached unless it is a necessary inference deducible from the evidence or circumstances of the case. The submission of the learned Deputy Attorney General, that as the accused-appellants assaulted the victim simultaneously one after another it is sufficient to hold that the accused-appellants developed a common intention to kill the deceased on the spur of the moment; cannot be accepted unless there are other materials from which inference of common intention can necessarily be reached. It may be mentioned in this connection that several persons can simultaneously attack a man and each can have same intention to kill, and each can individually inflict separate fatal blow and yet none would have the common intention as required by section 34 of the Penal Code because there was no prior meeting of minds to form a prearranged plan. In a case like that each would be individually liable for whatever injury he caused but none could be vicariously convicted for the act of the other, and if the prosecution cannot prove that his separate blow was fatal one, he cannot be convicted of the murder, however clearly his intention to kill could be proved in this case. Otherwise the unlamented section 34 of the Penal Code would have covered such a case without adding the words "in furtherance of common intention of all acts" to the section in 1870. That is why the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Mabhub Shah V s- Emperor gave the caution that care must be taken not to confuse same or similar intention with common intention and the partition which divides "their bounds" is very thin; nevertheless, the distinction is real and substantial and if overlooked will result in miscarriage of justice. Simply because several persons simultaneously attacked a man each having same intention to kill individually, inflicted separate blow, yet none would have the common intention required by section 34 of the Penal Code without further materials to prove their sharing of intention. 

 19. In Mahbub Shah's case the facts in short were that while Quasim Shah tried to prevent the complainant party from taking reeds Alladad struck Quasim Shah when he shouted out for help and Wali Shah and Mahbub Shah came with guns in their hands and when the complainant party tried to run away they came in front of them and Wali Shah fired at Alladad who fell down dead and Mahbub Shah fired at Hamid Shah causing injury to him. The question before the Privy council was whether Mahbub Shah was vicariously liable for causing the death of Alladad and their Lordships answered the question in the negative holding that there was no common intention as required under section 34 of the Penal Code. Similarly in the case of Ekabbar Ali -Vs- State (22 DLR 620) the facts were that on the order of Taher, Ekabbar dealt a blow on the head of Abdur Rashid with a 'Ish' (wooden part of a plough) when he fell down and thereafter Akkas dealt a fala blow on the left side of the belly and Taher gave a fala blow below the blow given by Akkas. The medical evidence was that the blow given by Taher was fatal. The question raised was whether Ekabbar and Akkas formed any common intention with Taher to murder Abdur Rashid on the spur of the moment and their Lordships of the Dhaka High Court held that there was no common intention developed on the spur of the moment. In the Privy Council case of Mamand -Vs- Emperor referred to earlier, the facts were that appellants 2 & 3 assaulted the deceased Naman with sticks and accused Mamand grappled with Chari and on the evidence on record their Lordships of the Privy Council found that ac- cussed Amman had enmity with Naman because of his relations with Fatima and inferred a common in-  tension of the accused; not because Mamand acted mutinously with appellants& 3 but because there was previous enmity with Namap, As such in that case there was material, over and above the simultaneous attack, In as much as there was evidence of enormity between the accused and the victim. In the case of Daye Moshya Bhil, State reported m AIR. 1-84- 1717 three persons chased the victim and Simultaneously attacked his causing injuries and the main accused was but the two tones causing moor to the victim. Confident he nature of the Junesthe Spurme Court of India held that there was no amongst the three accused as required under second 34 of the Penal Code. 

 20. In the case before us, although the prosecution has been able to prove that the accused appellants simultaneously attacked the victim but' there is no other material from which a necessary inference of common intention can be reached. Further the head injury has proved fatal and the injuries attributed to accused Sayeedur Rahman and accused Bakkar are of simple nature; and as such no inference of common intention is deducible from the nature of injuries inflicted upon the victim. In the instant case there is absolutely no evidence of a pre-concert or meeting of mind to cause the death of the deceased Tara. There is nothing on record to show that any of them shared the intention of the other in inflicting the injuries on the person of Tara which caused his death. There is also no material on record to suggest any animus or previous enmity between the accused appellants and the deceased Tara for which they might be actuated by a common intention to cause the injuries which have resulted in the death of Tara specially when Tara went to the place of. In these circumstances it is very difficult to hold that the accused-appellants assaulted the deceased in furtherance of any common intention of all. It is not impossible, as has been contended by Mr. Azizul Haque, that the accused appellants acted on their individual responsibility and although seemingly it might look to be a concerted action yet in fact they acted on their individual responsibility with the same or similar intention, but certainly not in furtherance of common intention of all. We are, therefore, inclined to hold that in the facts and circus stances of the case, the prosecution have failed to prove that there was a common intention of the accused appellants to cause the injuries which resulted in the death of the deceased Tara.
